video_title: Jon Havice, Founder and CIO, DGV Solutions
gist: Jon Havice of DGV Solutions walks Dean Curnutt through building institutional portfolios out of harvested risk premia: a CBOE-PutWrite-style S&P core running ~0.65 beta and a third less risk, carry-plus-value in FX (currently long yen at 158 against ~100 PPP fair value), carry-plus-momentum across 37 commodity instruments, and multi-asset trend as the hedge for slow bear markets that puts miss. His central warning is structural fragility: bailouts have scaled 100x per decade toward a possible $20 trillion need against $39 trillion of US debt, with passive flows, 6-7x levered pod shops and hair-trigger risk management making the VIX far more reactive.

insights.claim: US charitable foundations must clear roughly 7.5% annually to survive in perpetuity — 5% mandatory spend plus ~2% CPI plus ~50bps of administrative cost — which is the real hurdle any product sold to that channel must beat.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Sets the minimum return bar for any strategy marketed to endowments/foundations; products yielding less than ~7.5% net are structurally unsellable to that buyer.
insights.quote: So I don't know if inflation's 2% you're talking about 5 plus 2 plus 50 basis points and you got to get to 7 and a half%.

insights.claim: Endowment and foundation portfolios have a 'stability preference' that is as binding as the return target, because a 30% drawdown forces the institution to renege on multi-year grant commitments to grantees.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Explains why this buyer pays up for volatility reduction rather than maximum expected return — the demand for drawdown-controlled beta is a mandate constraint, not a preference.
insights.quote: The last thing you want to do is have this portfolio that lurches around where you say, "Oh, you know, one year we make hay and we're up 30%, the next year we lose 30%."

insights.claim: DGV Solutions was founded in 2014 on the premise that hedge-fund-like exposures delivered systematically require low headcount and can therefore be priced far below the 2-and-20 model.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Fee compression via systematic replication is the business model here — a structural threat to discretionary managers selling the same risk premia.
insights.quote: if you have low headcount, you can offer your products at a, you know, a very reasonable price

insights.claim: Private equity's original edge — buying private businesses at ~5x EBITDA and applying financial engineering — has been competed away by capital inflows, pushing the search for edge toward less-covered areas like commodity relative value.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Argues forward PE returns are structurally lower than the 1980s-90s vintage; capital crowding is the mechanism to watch for any strategy.
insights.quote: you could buy private businesses at you know five times I ebida and do some financial engineering

insights.claim: From 1986 to 2016 the CBOE PutWrite index outperformed the S&P 500 on annualized return while running about 35% less volatility, which is why mean-variance optimizers allocate to it over passive index exposure.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A public, replicable benchmark that has historically dominated the S&P on risk-adjusted terms — the base case for substituting putwriting for long-only equity beta.
insights.quote: if you look from 1986 to 2016, the SIBO putright index actually outperformed the S&P 500 on a outright kind of annualized return basis, but it did it with about 35% less volatility

insights.claim: The CBOE PutWrite index is deliberately crude — it rolls only once a month, 12 times a year — leaving room for an active systematic manager to beat it by choosing which puts are richest.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The published index is a floor, not a ceiling; the alpha claim is in strike/tenor selection, so due diligence should focus there.
insights.quote: It traded, you know, once a month, you know, 12 times a year. And you know, if if you're savvy with options, we figured we could beat that.

insights.claim: DGV guided investors to 0–4% of excess return over the CBOE PutWrite index and says realized results have landed inside that band.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable alpha budget for systematic putwriting — useful as a benchmark for competing products.
insights.quote: we we guided investors that we could do 0 to 4% over that index over time and you know, our our returns have been in that

insights.claim: DGV's putwrite program runs at roughly 0.65 beta to the S&P 500, so it lags in 20%-annualizing bull markets (up 17-18 instead) but should lose only 10-15% when the index falls 30%.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Quantifies the trade-off precisely — the strategy is a convexity-for-upside swap, and its underperformance in melt-ups is a feature to be underwritten, not a failure.
insights.quote: the one the way we do it runs at about a 065 beta to the S&P 500

insights.claim: The whole DGV fund, including all overlays, is engineered to run about a third less risk than the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Risk target that frames how the overlays are sized — diversifiers are added without adding aggregate volatility.
insights.quote: our our fund runs at even with the the overlays that we've put on a third less risk than the S&P 500

insights.claim: The volatility risk premium is structurally the same trade as property insurance: an actuarially fair S&P crash policy would cost $5,000 on a $500,000 house, but the market clears nearer $7,500 because sellers must be paid for capital, claims processing and administration.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Gives a transferable model for sizing what the VRP should pay — and for spotting when the spread compresses below the cost of bearing the risk.
insights.quote: nobody wakes up in the morning and says gosh you know what I I really want to sell crash protection on the S&P 500

insights.claim: The reliable payoff in short-volatility is not avoiding the shock but surviving it, because premiums always expand on the far side — the VIX going from 15 to 80 lets a surviving seller re-write at far richer levels and recoup the loss.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The entire edge is conditional on staying solvent through the event; sizing discipline, not forecasting, is the alpha driver in short-vol.
insights.quote: But what always happens on the backside of the hurricane is premiums expand.

insights.claim: In 2017, the lowest-volatility year in history, the VIX averaged about 10.5 while realized S&P volatility came in near 6.5, so the ~4-point volatility risk premium was fully intact even at record-low absolute levels.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Kills the 'vol is too low to sell' reflex — the premium is a spread, not a level, and can persist at VIX 10 as readily as at VIX 30.
insights.quote: Lowest volatility, you know, year in history. the I think the VIX averaged 10 and a half in 2017. The amazing thing is is real realized volatility came in at like six and a half.

insights.claim: Measured in percentage terms the 2017 premium was actually the same as normal: 4 points on a 20 implied is 20%, and at 10 implied a 20% premium implies 8 realized versus the 6 that actually printed.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The right way to normalize VRP across regimes is proportional, not absolute — a screen that flags 'only 4 vol points' misreads low-vol regimes.
insights.quote: if we're starting at 10 is implied 20%, you said we should have realized eight and really we realized six

insights.claim: DGV made money through 2020 as a short-volatility participant, because the ability to sell at an 80 VIX and recapture premium as it collapsed offset the crash loss within the same year.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: A live proof-of-concept that a properly capitalized short-vol book can be net positive in a tail year — the discriminator is capitalization, not the strategy label.
insights.quote: You guys made it through 2020 as a shortv uh market participant with a gain.

insights.claim: The options market functions as a forward-looking aggregation device around known event dates — elections, geopolitical events, payroll prints — so implied vol embeds crowd expectations, and the systematic seller's job is to be the consistent counterparty.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Frames event-vol as a persistent risk-transfer opportunity rather than a forecasting contest.
insights.quote: the the options market is like this um eye of Sauron that can somehow see into the future

insights.claim: The behavioural root of the VRP is that people systematically overpay for asymmetric payoffs: a Powerball ticket theoretically worth ~60 cents consistently sells for $2.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: If the driver is a hardwired human bias rather than a market inefficiency, the premium should not be arbitraged away — supporting persistence of the trade.
insights.quote: power ball is you know depending on the jackpot size might theoretically be worth 60 cents but people consistently paid $2 for for the lottery ticket

insights.claim: Ross Stevens' University of Chicago research found the horse-racing longshot premium is not constant — bettors overpay progressively more through the day, peaking in the last race as losing bettors chase to get even.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: Implies the demand for lottery-like payoffs intensifies after losses — a testable analogue for late-session and post-drawdown call/put skew richness.
insights.quote: he found that over time you pay even more up for it in other words throughout the day and then the very last race of the day it goes up a tremendous amount

insights.claim: The volatility risk premium is no longer a secret trade — a wave of retail ETFs including YieldMax has commoditized it, and buy-write is now the most popular option strategy in the world.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Crowding in the naive expression (buy stock, sell OTM call) argues for edge in implementation rather than in the raw premium; also flags flow-driven distortion in single-stock vol.
insights.quote: the buy rate is probably the most popular option strategy in the world

themes.theme: FX: Carry Anchored by Value, and the Yen

insights.claim: Momentum does not work in developed-market FX — the euro sits about 3 cents from where it launched 27 years ago — so DGV deliberately runs carry and value in currencies and ignores trend.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A direct instruction on factor placement: trend-following capital deployed in G10 FX is likely mispositioned.
insights.quote: in the developed market FX momentum doesn't really work

insights.claim: The euro was incepted on 1 January 1999 near 1.1850 and trades near 1.1530 today — roughly 3 cents of change in 27 years — evidence that major currency blocs are far more anchored than headline volatility suggests.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Argues for mean-reversion/value framing in G10 crosses and against structural directional bets on the dollar-euro axis.
insights.quote: In January 1st of 1999 when the euro was incepted, it came in at about 11850 was where the exchange rate was.

insights.claim: Carry trades fail in a characteristic way: they build up, attract leverage, feed on their own success, and then unwind abruptly when a shock forces capital home — which is why value must be layered on as a governor.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A reusable positioning rule — carry exposure should be scaled down precisely as the trade becomes crowded and valuation-stretched, not up.
insights.quote: The challenge with the carry trade is they they tend to build up over time. People get in them, they work, they they feed the beast, they put more money into it or they leverage them.

insights.claim: Value in currencies is best proxied by purchasing power parity, and the Economist's latest Big Mac index puts the burger at $6.20 in the US against $3 in Japan — implying the yen is roughly half price.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Gives a hard, current PPP anchor for the yen — a concrete valuation input for anyone sizing yen exposure.
insights.quote: Big Mac in the US cost $6.20. In Japan it costs $3, right?

insights.claim: Purchasing power parity fair value on dollar-yen is around 100 while spot trades at 158, and the yen has moved from as strong as 78 to 158 — a valuation gap DGV considers overwhelming.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Quantifies the magnitude of yen undervaluation being used to override a carry signal — a roughly 35% gap to model fair value.
insights.quote: the fair value purchasing power parody of dollar yen is really at like a 100 and it's trading at 158 today

insights.claim: DGV is long the Japanese yen, accepting the negative carry of giving up 4.5% US Treasuries versus 2% JGBs, because the value factor now dominates the carry factor in its models.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: An explicit, currently-held position with a stated cost of carry — the trade is a valuation bet with a known negative carry drag.
insights.quote: we uh we like the Japanese yen because the the value factor is really overwhelming in our analysis

insights.claim: The US Treasury joined the Bank of Japan last week in intervening in dollar-yen after it reached about 163, knocking it back to roughly 155-156 on Sunday night — and the guest suspects ulterior motives behind US participation.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Joint US-Japan intervention is a regime change in yen policy risk; short-yen carry positions now face official-sector opposition, not just valuation drag.
insights.quote: the US Treasury joined uh the BOJ last week in intervening in dollar yen. It got up to about 163 and change. They knocked it down to about 156 155 on Sunday night.

insights.claim: Japan's authorities hold roughly $1.1 trillion of US Treasuries as a rational response to domestic rates being artificially suppressed — the same logic that drives the private carry trade.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Frames official Japanese Treasury holdings as a carry position that can reverse for the same reasons private carry does — a channel for a disorderly US rates move.
insights.quote: we're going to hold $1.1 trillion of of US treasuries because, you know, our money is treated better in the US than it is in Japan

insights.claim: When a currency reaches roughly 50% undervaluation, real-economy arbitrage takes over — capital moves in, leveraged buyouts of Japanese assets become attractive, and tourists reprice the gap, which is the mechanism that pulls FX back to fair value.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Identifies the concrete transmission channel for FX mean reversion — watch inbound M&A and tourism flows into Japan as confirming evidence.
insights.quote: The the yen gets 50% overvalued in in time. You would say people will just move money. They'll they'll do leverage buyouts in Japan or or whatever.

insights.claim: Structural FX crisis frequency has fallen because the Asian pegs that broke in the late 90s have been replaced by large reserve buffers and export surpluses, and because the euro absorbed the perennial troublemakers like the lira and peseta.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Explains persistently low G10 FX vol as structural rather than cyclical — argues against buying long-dated G10 FX volatility on mean-reversion grounds.
insights.quote: some of the peripheral troublemakers over the years, you know, the the Italian LRA, the Spanish beta, those don't exist anymore

insights.claim: Systematic models should be overridden only for genuinely unmodelable events — DGV has done so a countable handful of times in 11 years, mostly for market closures like the day the exchanges shut for President Carter's funeral.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A concrete discipline benchmark for evaluating any systematic manager: override frequency near zero, and only for structural/unmodelable events.
insights.quote: I can in the last 11 years on one hand count the numbers of times where we've overridden our models

themes.theme: Commodity Carry, Momentum and the Energy Complex

insights.claim: In commodities the factor ranking inverts relative to FX: value is meaningless because prices are set by supply and demand, while carry is DGV's most powerful signal, overlaid with momentum.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A specific factor-allocation map — deploy value in FX, carry plus momentum in commodities; misapplying factors across asset classes destroys the edge.
insights.quote: in the commodity markets, you know, value doesn't really make sense. It's it's a commodity after all. It's all about supply and demand

insights.claim: Commodity carry is structurally identical to the VIX curve: normal contango means a third-month VIX bought at 19 rolls down toward a 16 spot, costing three points on a $19 investment over three months.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A single mental model unifying VIX and commodity roll — makes long-volatility and long-commodity carry costs directly comparable.
insights.quote: spot VIX is at 16. Third month VIX is at 19. We expect it to mean revert over time to 20

insights.claim: Backwardation is the tradeable inversion — during the recent Iran war the crude curve inverted, so buying the third month and rolling up the curve pays as long as the status quo holds.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Curve shape is the entry signal; a persistently backwardated energy curve is a positive-carry long, independent of a directional price view.
insights.quote: more recently here in the Iran war the the curve inverted right and you get this backradated curve

insights.claim: Momentum acts as the kill switch on commodity carry: if the curve stays backwardated but trend flips, DGV's models will exit the long and can flip outright short on the way down.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The combination avoids the classic carry blow-up — positive carry alone is not a reason to stay long into a downtrend.
insights.quote: if it starts to shift and the momentum signal flips our models will also flip and say we're we're not going to be long oil anymore

insights.claim: DGV runs its commodity carry-plus-momentum program across 37 different instruments, not just headline crude.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Breadth is the risk control — single-commodity trend expressions carry far more idiosyncratic risk than the diversified version.
insights.quote: So we do that across 37 different instruments.

insights.claim: Through the Iran conflict DGV was net long the energy complex despite being short crude itself — the gains came from distillates and from natural gas, which rallied because Qatar, one of the largest producers, was taken offline.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Shows why energy exposure should be modelled as a complex, not a single contract; the headline barrel can be the wrong leg entirely.
insights.quote: I think we were actually short oil but we were long some of the distillates and things like that that actually you know performed better

insights.claim: Volatility-targeting mechanically cut DGV's energy exposure roughly in half at rebalancing as the war raised realized vol, meaning the position rode crude from ~$70 to ~$100 at full size but only half size on the retrace to ~$85.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Vol-targeting is what converts a round-trip in price into a retained gain — an underappreciated source of return in trend programs.
insights.quote: you reduce your size by half and it runs back down to 85

insights.claim: Futures are the preferred implementation vehicle because they are cheap to capitalize — gold requires about 8% margin — allowing overlays to be ported on top of an existing beta exposure without new capital.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: This is the portable-alpha mechanic that lets a putwrite core and multiple diversifiers coexist in one dollar of client capital.
insights.quote: if you look at a gold future you know requires like 8% capital against it

themes.theme: Leverage Discipline and Anatomy of Blow-Ups

insights.claim: The cardinal sin of 36 years in derivatives is ever letting someone else take your positions away from you — a margin clerk, a prime broker, or a redeeming investor.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The single organizing principle for surviving short-vol; every capital structure decision should be tested against whether it preserves position control.
insights.quote: the one cardinal sin is ever letting anybody take your positions away from you

insights.claim: A large hedge fund playing the AI theme was over-levered and forced by its prime brokers to sell its portfolio to Citadel at a discount last week, reportedly taking a 67% loss without being fully wiped out.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A live, recent forced-deleveraging event in the AI complex — evidence that crowded AI exposure is now producing prime-broker-driven liquidations.
insights.quote: his prime brokers sort of moved to foreclose on him and he ended up, you know, selling his portfolio to Citadel at a at a discount

insights.claim: DGV's capital structure: $100 of client money goes into T-bills, $100 of S&P notional is written against roughly $7 of required margin, and all overlays — commodity RV, FX RV, trend, tail hedges — consume about another $3, leaving ~$90 unencumbered.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A transparent leverage disclosure allocators can replicate and compare — roughly 10% of capital encumbered is the benchmark for 'cannot be forced out'.
insights.quote: we have about $90 of unencumbered capital of the $100 that investor gave us

insights.claim: The common thread across LTCM, Howie Hubler, Victor Niederhoffer and the 2018 short-vol blow-ups is not model error but leverage and position size compounding into a trade that was already working.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Redirects diligence away from strategy critique and toward sizing policy — the failure mode is behavioural scaling, not the underlying edge.
insights.quote: Most of the time it comes back to leverage

insights.claim: Short-volatility arithmetic is brutally simple: short an instrument at 10 that goes to 20 and you lose 100% — which is exactly what happened to investors crowded into XIV during the 2017 low-vol regime.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A back-of-envelope check on any short-vol exposure — the loss is proportional to the multiple of the entry level, so low entry vol is maximally dangerous, not safe.
insights.quote: if if you're short an instrument at 10 right volatility or otherwise uh and it goes to 20, you know, you lose 100%

insights.claim: The classic single-stock put-selling failure is scaling: a seller comfortable at $100 notional on Nvidia 200-strike puts sees it work repeatedly and moves to $500, then meets an SK Hynix-style 50% drawdown at five times normal size.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Names the specific mechanism killing 'sell puts on stocks you'd own' programs — and flags that July already delivered the 50% semiconductor drawdown that punishes it.
insights.quote: my normal position size's $100 and this has been working. What if I do $500

insights.claim: The behavioural driver of over-sizing is 'emotional momentum' — adding to what has worked with risk limits be damned — which is why limits must be hard-coded before the trade, not judged in the moment.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Argues for pre-committed, mechanical position caps as the only reliable defence; discretionary limit-setting fails under profit.
insights.quote: there's that behavior element of you know it's like uh emotional momentum you know add to things that are working and you know risk limits be damned

insights.claim: Machine learning and unconstrained optimization give a false sense of security: a backtest may promise an extra 300bps annualized, but the path involves being 150% long S&P in mid-March 2020 — a position nobody would actually hold.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A concrete critique of AI-driven portfolio construction — inspect the extreme-position path of any optimized model, not just its return summary.
insights.quote: nobody wants to be 150% long in the middle of March in 2020, no matter what your models are saying

insights.claim: Mean-reversion models that buy more S&P after five consecutive down days must be stress-tested for whether the manager can psychologically hold the resulting size — the design test is 'will John take us out of this trade?'
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Behavioural capacity is a risk parameter to be modelled upfront; a model the manager will abandon under stress has no expected return.
insights.quote: can we stomach it where, you know, John is not going to take us out of this trade because, you know, this exposure got too big

insights.claim: Drawdowns come in two distinct shapes and require opposite hedges: the 1987 one-day 20% crash and COVID's 35% in 27 trading days were high-velocity events where short-dated OTM S&P puts returned many multiples of premium.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Hedge selection must be conditioned on the crash type you fear; buying convexity is only correct for velocity events.
insights.quote: your your best hedge in the 87 event or your best hedge in the 2020 event was very shortdated out of the money puts on the S&P 500

insights.claim: The 2000-2002 bear market fell 50% over two and a half years, during which a short-dated put program would have expired worthless throughout while the portfolio still lost half its value — insurance paid for, protection not delivered.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The strongest argument against a pure long-put tail program as a standalone hedge — the most damaging drawdown type is precisely the one puts miss.
insights.quote: You would have lost 50% in your underlying portfolio and paid a bunch of insurance premium along the way that provided no protection for you.

insights.claim: Trend following is the correct hedge for slow grinding declines because models flip short within about a month and then ride the trend down — which is why DGV layers multi-asset trend on top of its putwrite core.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Pairs two hedges with complementary crash-type coverage; a tail program without trend is only half-hedged.
insights.quote: What really works in that slow trending decline is trend following

insights.claim: DGV runs five separate 'optimized tail programs' designed to carry relatively efficiently while still delivering asymmetric payoff — an admission that a single tail expression cannot cover the outcome space.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Diversifying the tail sleeve itself is the design answer to unknowable crash shape; carry efficiency is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: we've got five what we think of as sort of optimized tail programs that are designed to carry relatively efficiently

insights.claim: Equity beta and the volatility risk premium are inversely correlated within a single portfolio — grinding bull markets pay the beta and starve the VRP, while corrections reverse it as the VIX moves from 15 to 35 or 55.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: This internal hedge is the reason putwriting reduces portfolio volatility rather than merely reducing return; the two return drivers offset by construction.
insights.quote: when when stocks are grinding higher, you know, you'll make more money on your beta and less money on your volatility risk premium because VSS are kind of low

insights.claim: The right form of diversification is by underlying return driver expressed across asset classes, not the traditional 60/40-plus-real-assets split.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to conventional allocation — the unit of diversification should be the risk premium, not the asset label.
insights.quote: not so much in the traditional diversification of like, hey, I'm going to have 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds

insights.claim: Crisis bailout size has scaled by roughly 100x per decade — $5 billion orchestrated for LTCM in 1998, $700 billion of TARP in 2008, and about $5 trillion of COVID relief in 2020.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The escalation series is the core of the fragility thesis — extrapolating it defines the size of the next required intervention.
insights.quote: the TARP bailout was $700 billion, right? So you you you go up a factor of 100 in 10 years

insights.claim: The next crisis, arriving on the roughly decadal cadence, could require a $20 trillion bailout against $39 trillion of existing US debt — and the market may simply not be there to fund it.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The central macro tail risk articulated in this episode: the buyer of last resort's own balance sheet becomes the binding constraint.
insights.quote: in 2030, is the next crisis going to require not a $5 trillion bailout, but maybe a $20 trillion bailout? Is the market there when we already have, you know, $39 trillion of debt to do that?

insights.claim: The defining event of the next cycle will be the market discovering that the buyer of last resort has no clothes — a regime where the Fed/Treasury put itself is repriced.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: If credible, every strategy that implicitly relies on the policy put — short vol, levered credit, duration — is mispriced for that state.
insights.quote: the buyer of last resort has no clothes. And that's a real problem. And I don't think we're there yet.

insights.claim: The UK is the live preview of fiscal constraint in a G7 economy: any attempt at fiscal spend makes gilt yields explode higher, forcing austerity.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Gilts are the leading indicator for the bond-vigilante regime the guest expects to spread; watch UK fiscal events as the template.
insights.quote: every time they try to to do anything like on a fiscal spend, guilt yields explode higher

insights.claim: Host and guest converge on an 11-year crisis cadence — 1987, 1998 LTCM, 2009 S&P low, 2020 COVID — putting the next major event at 2031, roughly five years out.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit date stamp for the thesis; a planning horizon for building genuinely durable portfolio structure.
insights.quote: So instead of 2030, I got it marked at 2031.

insights.claim: The rise of passive investing has removed the discriminating bid — flows are 'student body left, student body right' with no one stepping in to buy a specific mispriced name.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Structural explanation for why dislocations run further and faster; supports owning convexity rather than relying on value buyers to appear.
insights.quote: It's more student body left, student body right. You know, it's like, hey, I own the S&P, sell the S&P, and there's no discrimination.

insights.claim: Pod-shop multi-strategy funds levered six or seven times on $50-100 billion of capital run hair-trigger risk management — capital halved at a 5% pod drawdown, fired at 10% — which converts sophisticated risk control into a synchronized cascade.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific mechanism behind modern flash-deleveraging; positions correlated with pod-shop books carry hidden liquidation risk.
insights.quote: most of those funds are levered six or seven times on 50 to hundred billion dollars of capital and they say like we're hitting the exit very quickly

insights.claim: Just-in-time risk management has made the VIX far more reactive — a 5% S&P move on a minor headline can now take the VIX from 17 to 39.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: Vol-of-vol has structurally risen; short-vol sizing must assume much larger VIX gaps per unit of index move than historical betas imply.
insights.quote: the VIX just went from, you know, 17 to 39 on a 5% move in the S&P 500

insights.claim: AI is widening the distribution of outcomes for markets and society — with Musk/Huang Mars-and-universal-high-income utopia on the right tail and mass technological unemployment on the left — and the guest leans right of centre while insisting the width itself is the investable fact.
insights.speaker: Jon Havice
insights.so_what: The actionable conclusion is not a directional AI bet but higher diversification and more convexity, because outcome variance has risen.
insights.quote: this artificial intelligence is broadening the spectrum of potential outcomes uh for both markets and I think for society
